before: The main document treated Sarvam's models as reference points only — data for token counts (Sarvam-105B on 12T, Sarvam-30B on 16T, §1.1) and for tokenizer fertility of 1.4–2.1 (§1.3) — and §16 planned a 300B trained from scratch.
after: Sarvam-105B and Sarvam-30B are Apache 2.0 with full architecture disclosed on their Hugging Face model cards: 105B with 10.3B active, 128 experts with top-8 routing, 1 shared expert, MLA-style decoupled QK (q_head_dim 192, v_head_dim 128, head_dim 576, hidden_size 4096), YaRN scaling factor 40 at 128K, auxiliary-loss-free router balancing, 12T pre-training tokens. That is a licence-free starting position, not a reference point, and it opens three options that did not exist in the main document's framing: upcycle a 105B Apache-2.0 checkpoint toward ~300B, distil it as an Indic teacher with zero licence-chain contamination, or benchmark against it honestly.
why: Licence and architecture were read directly from the model cards. A free Apache-2.0 105B MoE with an Indic-optimised tokenizer, already strong on agentic and coding tasks, is now the bar any 300B must beat — and it is the clean alternative to BhashaKritika's bespoke Krutrim Community Licence (§3.4), which the main document said you would otherwise have to replicate yourself. The addendum recommends a 2-week evaluation of Sarvam-105B on the target task set before committing capital: if it lands within ~10% on Indic tasks, the case for a from-scratch 300B rests entirely on coding/agentic/English headroom.
source: Hugging Face model cards `sarvamai/sarvam-105b` and `sarvamai/sarvam-30b`; https://www.sarvam.ai/blogs/sarvam-30b-105b (public rollout 6 March 2026)

before: §9.2: "Fine-tuning olmOCR for Devanagari, Bengali, Tamil, Telugu and Perso-Arabic scripts is arguably the highest-ROI engineering project in this whole plan." §17 lists olmOCR/olmOCR-2 as the OCR tool to adopt rather than rebuild, §18.1 makes it the mitigation for the Indic-OCR risk, and §19 item 6 budgets weeks 4–10 for it.
after: Do not use olmOCR for Devanagari. On 300 real printed Hindi/Devanagari scans, olmOCR-7B falls to 40.5 chrF++ — the worst-in-class result of ten systems, from the model behind olmOCR-Bench. Build the Indic OCR pipeline on Qwen3-VL-8B instead, the best open model at 75.2, which beats GPT-5.5 (58.5) and runs on a single 24 GB GPU. Report median and catastrophic-failure rate, never mean, and validate exclusively on real scans.
why: A ten-system stress test showed that on clean rendered text all ten cluster at chrF++ 91–98 — synthetic text does not separate systems at all, so any vendor benchmark using rendered text is meaningless — while on real scans nine of ten collapse across a 76-point range (EasyOCR 93.6 → 58.3). Strong English OCR does not predict Indic OCR. DeepSeek-OCR has the best median of any system but rare catastrophic repetition failures (outputs up to 71× reference length) destroy its mean. The addendum states the correction "is worth months of misdirected effort".
source: arXiv:2606.29213 — "Can OCR-VLMs Read Devanagari? A Stress-Test Benchmark and Post-Correction Study", published 28 June 2026

before: §1.3 listed tokenizer fertility as one of three things that will determine whether the model is good, asserted that "your tokenizer decision is worth more than 2T extra tokens", and told you to "budget a dedicated workstream". §18.1 rated it a High technical risk with the same workstream mitigation.
after: Elevate the tokenizer from a workstream to a gating milestone — nothing else should start until fertility is validated across all 22 scripts. The penalty is now measured: Indian languages pay an average 8.0× tokenization tax versus English under cl100k_base, reaching 13.0× for Malayalam, which reduces the effective context window to as little as 12% of what English users get for equivalent semantic content. The mechanism is identified and remediable — failed byte-pair merges leaving text fragmented into single-byte tokens, with merge failure correlating with tax at Pearson r = 0.89 — and XLM-R and o200k_base already reduce the average Indic tax by 73%.
why: The main document's #1 priority was an assertion; it is now backed by measurement on FLORES-200 across six tokenizers and fourteen Indian languages, with an identified mechanism. The finding also reframes the problem: "This is not a property of Indic scripts — it is a tokenizer design failure." §B.3 adds that because o200k already removes 73% of the tax, the retrofit path (BrahmicTokenizer-131K + Kronecker embeddings) starts closer to the goal than the main report assumed.
source: arXiv:2607.24276 — "The Tokenizer Tax", 27 July 2026; companion arXiv:2607.23319 — "BHARATI", 25 July 2026

before: §8.2: "You have ~35,000+ hours of open, permissively-licensed Indic speech across IndicVoices + Vaani + SPRING-INX + Shrutilipi + Kathbath + SYSPIN." §19 item 5 budgets weeks 4–8 to ASR-transcribe "all 35K hours".
after: BhasaAnuvaad alone is ~44,400 hours plus 17M aligned text segments across 13–14 Indian languages and English, under CC BY 4.0. The total open Indic speech pool across BhasaAnuvaad + IndicVoices + Vaani + SPRING-INX + Shrutilipi + Kathbath + SYSPIN + Rasa is well north of 100,000 hours.
why: The main document omitted BhasaAnuvaad entirely, understating the open Indic speech pool by roughly 3×. Since §8 calls ASR transcription "one of the only ways to manufacture genuinely natural Indic text at scale", the transcription programme and its projected text yield scale with the corrected figure.
source: arXiv:2411.04699 · github.com/AI4Bharat/BhasaAnuvaad

before: §7 described BPCC as the "largest public Indic parallel corpus; all 22 languages", without quantifying it.
after: BPCC is ~230 million bitext pairs across all 22 scheduled languages.
why: The main document's entry was unquantified; the addendum supplies the figure from AI4Bharat's own NMT project page.
source: ai4bharat.iitm.ac.in/areas/nmt

before: §7 listed Samanantar at "~50M sentence pairs, 11 Indic languages".
after: 49.7M pairs across 11 Indic languages, of which 37.4M were newly mined.
why: Precision: the rounded ~50M figure is replaced with the published count, and the newly-mined share is added.
source: ai4bharat.iitm.ac.in/areas/nmt

before: §7 listed BPCC's licence as "CC-BY-4.0 ✅".
after: More precise, and cleaner than stated: BPCC-Mined, NLLB-Seed, ILCI, MASSIVE and BPCC-BT are released under CC0 — "no rights reserved". AI4Bharat waived all rights to the packaging.
why: The blanket CC-BY-4.0 characterisation understated how permissive the components actually are; CC0 removes even the attribution obligation for those subsets.
source: github.com/ai4bharat/IndicTrans2 (repo licence table)

before: §17 listed IndicTrans2 (AI4Bharat, all 22 languages, MIT) as the translation tool to adopt, and §7/§16 built the synthesis plan around it.
after: IndicTrans3-beta now exists, with document-level MT. For speech, IndicSeamless — SeamlessM4T-v2 fine-tuned on BhasaAnuvaad — is SOTA for Indic speech-to-text translation, beating cascaded approaches on both FLEURS and BhasaAnuvaad-test.
why: The main document's tooling table was one generation behind, and the cascaded ASR-then-MT approach it implies for speech is no longer the best option.
source: AI4Bharat Hugging Face org

before: §8.1 covered Indic TTS thinly — IndicTTS (IIT Madras, 13 languages, research-use 🟡) and SYSPIN (900+ hours, 9 languages) — with no all-22-language open TTS or ASR named.
after: TTS and ASR coverage is materially better than stated: Rasa (500+ hours of expressive studio speech, 20 speakers, 13 languages), IndicParler-TTS (the first open TTS covering all 22 languages, with prompt-controlled style), IndicF5 (11 languages), and IndicConformer (ASR for all 22).
why: The addendum records the main document's TTS coverage as "understated"; these releases change what is available off the shelf for the multimodal and ASR-transcription workstreams.
source: AI4Bharat Hugging Face org

before: Not mentioned anywhere in the main document.
after: The FBI and CIA datasets (AI4Bharat) exist, for building and testing multilingual LLM *evaluators*.
why: They are relevant to the recommendation to build a private Indic evaluation set — an evaluator you can trust is a prerequisite for the uncontaminated measuring instrument §12.3 Rule 4 asks you to commission.
source: AI4Bharat Hugging Face org

before: §16 budgeted the corpus in unique tokens seen once: ~0.3T naturally-occurring Indic tokens exist, therefore natural Indic can only be ~2.0% of a 15T mix ("that ratio is uncomfortable and it is also unavoidable"), the 40–70% dedup loss is the single most likely schedule-breaker (§18.1), and the 20T milestone requires "aggressive multi-epoch reuse" left hand-waved.
after: Budget in unique pool × deliberate epoch schedule = effective tokens. ~0.3T unique natural Indic × 4 epochs ≈ 1.2T effective at roughly zero quality cost, with a theoretical ceiling of ~4.8T effective at 16× — raising the natural-Indic effective share from ~2% to ~7–8% without collecting a single new token. Two-to-four epochs on the highest-quality tiers (FineWeb-Edu, curated-clean) is cheap and standard. The dedup risk is half-defused: dedup down to the unique pool, then choose repetition deliberately, because dedup ≠ see-once. The 20T milestone becomes principled and quantified — ~11–13T unique plus a scheduled epoch plan concentrated on the scarce, high-value tiers.
why: The section-16 math was "Chinchilla-brained": it silently assumed every token is seen once. Muennighoff et al. measured that up to 4 epochs of repeated data is almost as good as fresh data — an 8.7B model trained 4 epochs on 44B unique tokens finished with only 0.5% higher validation loss than a single-epoch model on 178B unique tokens — with a decay constant R*_D ≈ 15, worthlessness at 40 epochs, a hard ceiling at U·(1+R*_D) ≈ 16× the unique pool, and an allocation rule that when data-constrained you scale epochs faster than parameters. Two honest limits attach: the measurements are English web data at ≤9B parameters, and nobody has measured R*_D for Indic, translated or synthetic text; and repetition works on whole tiers, not slivers (up-sampling 0.1% of a corpus 100× significantly degrades performance).
source: arXiv:2305.16264 — Muennighoff et al., "Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models" (in-project); arXiv:2401.00448 — Sardana & Frankle, cited at thesis level only

before: §17's pipeline treated the mixture as static and phase-scheduled (§16.3), and considered neither what a per-iteration data selector costs at scale nor what an English-trained quality classifier does to Indic data.
after: Static phase-scheduled mixing is confirmed as the production backbone — it is what the only in-project 120B run actually shipped with. Add an Always-ON lane: ~8% of every batch reserved for Tier-2/3 Indic scripts, agentic/world-model traces and benchmark training splits, bypassing every selector and quality classifier. Demote dynamic selection to ablation-stage tooling, never with an English-heavy reference proxy, and evaluate DataOrchestra for the *cleaning* stage instead of the selection stage.
why: LightningLM's golden proxy was English-heavy (cosine 0.876 with the English web band), so OPUS systematically under-valued Indic data and would have rejected it — "a single selector should not govern data whose value it cannot see". FineWeb-Edu-style quality classifiers carry exactly the same bias, so the Always-ON lane is the mechanism that guarantees Bodo, Santali, Dogri and Manipuri actually train at every stage. The economics also do not hold up: OPUS cost ~17% wall-clock throughput at the 5B stage in a sharded stack (30,429 vs 36,737 tok/s) against the 4.7% its own paper reports, and was disabled at 2B and again from 9B onward. The document marks this a 🔴 REVISION, though not one of the three labelled MATERIAL CORRECTIONs.
source: arXiv:2606.07404 — LightningLM 0.1V technical report (in-project); arXiv:2607.24717 — DataOrchestra, 28 July 2026

before: The main document framed the programme as which 300B to train from scratch — §1.2 recommends architecting for 15T tokens, and §16/§19 sequence a from-scratch run.
after: The $1B question is not "which 300B do we train" but "scratch vs grow", and the burden of proof now sits on scratch. Insert, before any capital commitment, a 4-week head-to-head at ~2B scale: from-scratch on your mix versus grown/upcycled, on identical data, judged on Indic + code held-out loss.
why: LightningLM grew a 120B sparse MoE (460 routed experts, top-12 routing, 5.93B active ≈ 5% of 118.67B stored) in four stages from a 1.78B dense seed, trained end-to-end on a single eight-GPU node at ~67 days and ~$100K-class economics; Grove-MoE upcycled Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base into a 33B MoE; and Sarvam-105B is Apache 2.0 with its full MoE recipe on the model card (X01). Growing inherits both the tokenizer and Indic competence at a large multiple less pre-training cost. For calibration, Llama 4 trained on >30T tokens and Qwen3 on 36T across 119 languages — the 15T target is respectable but not frontier-scale, which is why the effective-token and growth machinery matter more than raw collection.
source: arXiv:2606.07404 — LightningLM 0.1V (in-project); Grove-MoE (in its reference list); Hugging Face model cards per §A.1; in-project Topic-3 notes

before: §6: "Indic math/STEM is essentially absent."
after: Amend to "nearly absent": PatiGonit22K exists — 22,441 Bengali math word problems, simple through multi-operation, translated, annotated, culturally adapted and verified. The generate-and-translate strategy of §6 still stands, since this is roughly four orders of magnitude below MegaMath.
why: A category the main document said was empty turned out not to be, as of the 28 July 2026 cs.CL announcement. The document marks the row 🟡 "Corrects the report" and keeps the strategic conclusion unchanged because of the scale gap.
source: arXiv:2607.22859 — PatiGonit22K, announced 28 July 2026

before: The mix engine computed effective tokens as unique pool x epochs, a plain multiplication, and chapter 2 rendered the product as the value of a repetition schedule. Its ladder ran to 20 passes over a 336B natural-Indic pool and displayed 6.72T, badged UNEVIDENCED on the grounds that "published work stops at 16". The rail said nobody had measured repetition for Indian text.
after: Seen tokens and worth tokens are now separate quantities. Seen stays linear, because that is what compute is billed on. Worth follows Muennighoff et al. (JMLR v26, 2025) Eq. 18: D' = U + 15.4.U.(1 - e^(-(passes-1)/15.4)). Four passes are worth 3.73x rather than 4x, sixteen 10.6x rather than 16x, forty 15.2x rather than 40x, and no schedule exceeds 16.4x the unique pool. The 6.72T figure was not unevidenced but unreachable: the ceiling for a 336B pool is 5.51T at any number of passes. 16 epochs is the half-life at which a repeated token has lost 1/e of its value, not the end of the evidence — the same paper reports 44-epoch runs and labels 40 epochs worthless. And ATLAS (ICLR 2026, 774 runs over MADLAD-400) fits the curve per language and finds Hindi's tail bends upward sooner than English, so the constants are the optimistic end for an Indic pool rather than the neutral one. A guardrail now errors on any schedule asking a pool for more than repetition can be worth.
why: The multiplication is correct for cost and wrong for value, and the word "effective" let a compute-side quantity stand in for a data-side claim — which is the exact shape of the "Chinchilla-brained" error this project had already corrected once in the other direction. Two of the surrounding statements were also false rather than merely optimistic. The strategic consequence is larger than the arithmetic: Kimi K2 measured ten epochs of raw repetition at ~23.8% against ~28.9% for ten rephrasings read once, and Kimi K3's pre-training section does not use the word epoch at all, rephrasing knowledge and mathematics corpora with fidelity verification instead. Re-reading is the weakest answer to a scarce pool that is still better than nothing; this page does not yet cost a rephrasing pipeline, which is the open question the correction leaves behind.
source: Muennighoff et al., Scaling Data-Constrained Language Models, JMLR v26 (2025), Eq. 18 and Fig. 1; ATLAS, ICLR 2026, arXiv:2510.22037; Kimi K2, arXiv:2507.20534; Kimi K3, arXiv:2607.24653 SS3.1; DeepSeek-V3, arXiv:2412.19437

before: The contamination gate tokenised with the regular expression `\w+`, and reported an index of 411,442 thirteen-word fingerprints over MILU's validation split, of which 56 items were too short for the full window. The page described a shingle as thirteen consecutive words and said that thirteen words agreeing by chance is not a thing that happens.
after: Tokenisation keeps Unicode combining marks and composes to NFC, so a word is a word in every script. The same corpus indexes to 126,044 fingerprints at eight window widths, and 1,090 of the 8,923 items - not 56 - are genuinely shorter than the thirteen-word window. The floor below which an item is refused rose from 5 to 6, because the example the code's own comment gives as too generic to index ("what is the capital of") is five words long. The browser demo carried the identical defect in its own tokeniser and now mirrors the pipeline, including the floor: it used to tell a reader that any question under thirteen words was unprotectable, which contradicted both the pipeline and the paragraph beneath it.
why: Python's `\w` matches letters, digits and underscore but not combining marks, and every Indic vowel sign, virama, anusvara and nukta is a combining mark. So `\w+` split every Indic word at every vowel sign and discarded the sign: five Hindi words became eleven consonant fragments. 91% of the indexed items are in Indic scripts and inflated by a mean factor of 2.58, so a "thirteen-word fingerprint" was roughly five real words of skeleton there - and the gate produced false positives that would have deleted clean training text. Measured against 203,388 held-out FLORES-200 sentences the old tokeniser collided with 5 of them, all Indic, all ordinary news prose; the corrected one collides with none. One of the five was the Malayalam for "the attack greatly affected relations between India and Pakistan" - three ordinary words that normalised to a full thirteen-token window. The loss would have been silent and would have fallen on the scarcest tier in the mixture, the one the protected lane exists to defend. The suite passed throughout: 174 tests, none of which had ever been run against text in the scripts the gate was built for.
source: Measured in this repository: dataframework/shingles.py, data/benchmarks/MILU.json (8,923 items) and data/corpora/flores200_dataset (203,388 held-out sentences)

before: The `sourcing`, `lifecycle` and `orphan_tiers` blocks each declared `provenance: "measured"` over every number inside them, including committed_tokens of 6.39T. Three figures in the browser did the same by hand, one of them a counterfactual - what the corpus would hold if the reader resolved blockers that have not been resolved. 115 fertility values claimed to be measured against a run id literally prefixed `pending-`, and `protocol_gaps` stated that three of six tokenizers were unavailable.
after: A derived number is no more measured than its least-measured input. The three blocks are estimated, because every token figure in them is a sum over the catalogue's size_tokens and not one of the 145 records carries a measured size - 24 are estimated and 121 unknown. Exact counts keep the mark they earned: sourcing.counts, record_counts and grades are still measured, because counting records in a catalogue we hold is a measurement and a miscount would be a bug rather than an estimate. The run-id substitution now walks every block instead of one, so no placeholder ships; `protocol_gaps` is computed from the run and reads 5 tokenizers measured and 1 unavailable.
why: The page tells the reader that the green underline means somebody ran it. Nobody had run the 6.39T, and the mark is worth nothing if it can be applied to a sum of estimates. The invariant that should have caught this could not: it let a `provenance` key at the top of a block cover every number beneath it at any depth, so one declaration exempted 404 numeric leaves. The fertility case was the same failure in a different shape - the guard asked only whether a source contained an "@", not whether the id it named was a real run. Four guards now check the claims rather than the shape of the claims, each watched failing before being trusted. Per-field typing of the mixed count-and-token blocks remains the deeper fix and is not done here: the blocks under-claim on their exact counts rather than over-claim on their sums, which is the safe direction of the two.
source: Measured in this repository: web/data.json, records/fertility.json, dataframework/

before: Three of the guards enforcing the five invariants could not fail. INV-1b's mutation proof built a string from an eval item and asserted the item was in it. INV-2's check asked `is_commercially_usable(grade)` inside `if grade == "X"`, and that function was `grade != "X"` - so it reduced to asserting that "X" equals "X". The leak scan looked only for synthetic fixtures that were never within reach of the pipeline. Separately, `score_gates` summed whatever keys it was handed, `coverage.py`'s exclusion clause could only ever fire for one capability, `mix.check` skipped its ceiling test in silence on a tier with no stated pool, and the page disclosed one of the two guardrails its own mixture breaches.
after: The guards test the claims rather than restating the implementations. INV-2 reads the shipped plan and asserts no grade-X id reaches a committed tier; its mutation commits one and watches the guard object. `is_commercially_usable` takes the record and requires an established licence, because unknown is not permission - which the rest of the framework says and this function contradicted. The leak scan runs the real benchmark corpus when it is present, and its proof runs the same scanner over a bundle carrying an item. `score_gates` counts only the five named gates. `coverage.py` separates a substring trap from an outright disqualifier, so the india-context exclusion runs for the first time: IndicMMLU-Pro no longer counts as an instrument for Indian worldview, because its own notes say it was translated. `mix.check` reports an unassessable tier instead of skipping it, errors on a negative schedule, and no longer raises on a null one. And the mixture's synthetic-Indic breach is stated on the page beside the protected-lane breach.
why: A guard that cannot fail is worse than no guard, because it produces the confidence of a passing suite without the fact of one. Two of the five invariants were in that state while the page told readers each ships with a test proving it fails when broken. The grading consequences were live rather than theoretical: a duplicated gate key could score 14 out of a stated maximum of 10 and buy a grade A, and a dataset with no established licence answered True to the one function INV-2 exposes. The coverage exclusion had never run at all, so a translated benchmark was being counted as evidence for the capability the model is named for. Disclosing one breach and not the other was the subtlest of these: it reads as candour while showing half the picture.
source: Measured in this repository: dataframework/, tests/, web/data.json

before: The opening paragraph called the corpus 17 trillion tokens because 16.8 was rounded to zero decimals, while every other mention said 16.8T. Chapter 4 said the mixture had eight tiers and ten tiers on one screen, beside a figure drawing ten bars. The glossary defined a rung as one of 5, 10, 15 or 20 trillion tokens - a ladder replaced by 3T/8T/16.8T/30T - and defined a pass as contributing four times the pool's size, which is the arithmetic X15 exists to retract. Chapter 13 said all four licence-blocked datasets were English corpora and planned against 35,000 hours of open Indic speech. The cost chapter priced a 15T run. Two figures were both numbered Fig. 9. Sarvam-30B was 30B in one register and 32B in another, and both cited the model cards for token counts the cards do not state.
after: Every count and figure quoted in prose is read from the record that holds it: the tier count, the ladder top, the rung set, the preference-to-demonstration ratio. The budget renders to one decimal. The glossary states that four passes cost four times the compute and are worth about 3.7 times the pool. Chapter 13 says none of the four is an Indic corpus - two are English-only, two are multilingual with unmeasured Indian partitions, which is why they cannot be budgeted against - and plans against the 100,000+ hours correction X04 established. `run_cost.py` recomputes the run from the shipping budget: 2.80M H100-hours and $5.6M, not 2.50M and $5.0M. Post-training is Fig. 7. Sarvam's counts match the model cards and the token citations point at the blog that states them. The legend says what grade A requires and that nothing reaches it, so "four are committable today" no longer reads against "A usable (0)".
why: Every one of these is the same defect: a number typed into a sentence beside data that later moved. It is the fourth time this class has been corrected here - the seed's text called a 3B model a dense 40B, the third growth stage claimed to add 80B parameters where it adds 32B, the changelog quoted the pre-X16 shingle count - so this correction fixes the cause rather than the instances: prose that quotes a count now reads it. Where a figure genuinely cannot be computed, a test asserts the two records agree. The cost record is the second derivation to be moved out of static JSON for exactly this reason, after the vocabulary trade.
source: Measured in this repository: web/data.json, records/, web/chapters.js

before: A grade was a score and nothing else. UNKNOWN and FAIL both contributed 0, deliberately, so a dataset scoring 5 with every gate measured and one scoring 5 with three gates never looked at received the same letter. Grade A was unreached and the page did not say why. `score_gates` also summed whatever keys it was handed, so a duplicated gate name could score 14 out of a stated maximum of 10 and buy an A.
after: A grade now states coverage as well as score. A requires all five gates scored and a score of at least 8; B requires at least three scored and at least 5. The reasoning string names how many were scored, every dataset ships a `gates_scored` count beside its grade, and the bundle carries a per-gate coverage tally. `score_gates` counts only the five named gates. The grade distribution is unchanged - B 14, C 116, X 15 - which is the point: the rule says what the letters already meant rather than reshuffling them.
why: The catalogue makes this concrete rather than hypothetical. Gate by gate, out of 145: provenance 144 scored, composition 6, contamination 1, yield 15, evidence 145. Evidence is PASS for every dataset because every catalogued dataset has been used by somebody, so it is two free points that discriminate nothing, and 125 of 145 records have two gates scored or fewer. For most of the corpus the only real signal is where the text came from. Grade A was therefore empty for a reason nobody had stated: not that nothing is good enough, but that nothing has been fully checked. The chapter now says so, and names the sharpest case - the contamination gate is scored on one dataset in the whole catalogue, and on none of the four the plan commits to. Those four clear licence, provenance and size; they are not datasets somebody finished checking, and a reader deciding whether to trust the plan needs that in front of them rather than derivable from an appendix.
source: Measured in this repository: dataframework/grade.py, web/data.json gate_coverage

before: The eight guardrails in `mix.py` were presented in one voice. The repetition constants cited a fitted curve to three significant figures; the composition constants cited nothing. `MAX_SYNTHETIC_SHARE_OF_INDIC = 0.50` carried the comment "past this, the 'Indic' tier is mostly manufactured text", which restates what 0.50 means and says nothing about why fifty. The page then reported the mixture breaching two of these lines without saying what kind of lines they were.
after: Every guardrail states its basis and how strong that basis is, and the bundle ships them so the page can show it. Four are published findings or a fitted curve from the repetition literature. One is adopted - the protected lane's 8% floor is what LightningLM reserved on its own corpus, not a measured optimum for this one. Three are asserted: the 20% lane ceiling has no source anywhere, the 1% minimum tier share is our own line loosely motivated by a finding about up-sampling 0.1% slivers, and the 50% synthetic cap appears once, in a risk register's mitigation column, phrased as "cap synthetic at ~50%" with no citation and no experiment. The strength maps onto provenance, so a measured guardrail wears the mark that means somebody ran it and an asserted one does not.
why: Pankaj asked where the 50% came from, which nothing in the code could answer. It came from docs/ATLAS.md risk R02 and it is a rule of thumb, and both lines this mixture crosses turn out to be in the asserted group. That does not excuse the breach - it changes what the breach means, from "we exceeded a measured limit" to "we exceeded a line we drew ourselves and have never tested". Presented identically, a judgment somebody wrote down and a constant somebody measured are indistinguishable to a reader, which is the confusion the rest of this page exists to prevent. One further gap surfaced while tracing it: R02 prescribes four mitigations against synthetic collapse and only the cap is implemented - the KenLM-perplexity floor, the n-gram diversity floor and the per-language entropy monitor are recorded as prose and checked by nothing. The page now says that too.
source: docs/ATLAS.md risk R02; arXiv:2606.07404; arXiv:2305.16264; dataframework/mix.py

before: Chapter 2 took its pool from the mixture's `unique_tokens` field and said of it: "Read once, this is the entire natural Indian-language pool - every verified corpus anyone has assembled, added together." At the recommended budget that field is 336B. The chapter's whole argument followed from it: the pool is large, four passes are nearly free, so the Indian share is reachable.
after: The pool is summed from the catalogue, the same source the datasets chapter reads: 84.9B, being Sangraha's verified portion and IndicCorp v2. The field is renamed `unique_tokens_required` everywhere, because that is what it is. Chapter 2 now says four passes on the real pool are worth 316B - 24% of what the tier is allocated - and that filling the allocation takes about 16 passes, which is the half-life the published fit names, at which the tokens are worth 66% of what they cost.
why: `unique_tokens` was never a measurement. milestones.py computes it as share x budget / epochs, so at 16.8T the indic-natural tier's 8% share over 4 epochs produced 336B: the pool the mixture would need in order for the share it wants to work. A demand figure wearing the clothes of a supply figure, and the page stated it as an inventory in the most explicit words available. Two things hid it. The growth chapter had it right all along - "336B of unique natural Indian text this stage asks for, 4.0x SHORT" - so the page contradicted itself across two chapters with the same number. And risk R19 records a 250-500B estimate for the real pool, which 336B sits inside, so the figure looked corroborated; R19 also calls that estimate "the single most important unverified number in the entire document". The agreement was a coincidence of arithmetic. The corrected chapter is a stronger one: "nearly free" was true of a pool four times larger than the one anybody holds.
source: dataframework/milestones.py; web/data.json sourcing; records/risks.json R19

before: The page recorded, in correction X15, that repetition is the weakest answer to a scarce pool and that the frontier rephrases instead - and then went on planning around passes, because nobody had costed the alternative. Chapter 2 ended on how many times to read the pool. Chapter 13's queue did not mention rephrasing at all.
after: The rephrasing route is costed and carried in both chapters. Restating the 84.9B committable pool twice makes it 170B and lifts what the tier is worth by about 25% at identical seen tokens, for a generation cost that stays under 1% of the run however the throughput is estimated. Chapter 2 says so where it used to end on passes; chapter 13 prices it beside the speech route, with its three limits.
why: The finding is that it is worth doing and is not the answer. At two variants - the only depth Kimi K2 uses in production - the tier is still 13% filled by unique text and 87% by repetition. Filling it with unique text would take sixteen variants, past anything anybody has reported. And whether a rephrasing counts as a distinct document for the repetition curve has never been measured; the 25% assumes it does, and nothing published says what the penalty is if it does not. So the honest conclusion is that the cheapest real lever improves the slice and leaves the gap, which makes it the strongest argument for funding collection - the argument that survives having tried the alternative. Cost is shown as a band rather than a figure, with the arithmetic stated: the throughput term spans an order of magnitude because decode is bound by weight reads rather than FLOPs, so a point estimate would claim a precision this project does not have.
source: arXiv:2507.20534 (Kimi K2); arXiv:2607.24653 (K3); Muennighoff Eq. 18 applied here

before: Supply was reported as raw sums of dataset token counts. The page printed 61T reachable and 363% of budget, 54.6T unlocked by four letters, and 84.9B of committable natural Indic. Nemotron-CC (v1) sat in one list and Nemotron-CC-v2 in another and both were added. The code row recorded 377M tokens.
after: Every sum over catalogue tokens now reports what survives deduplication as well as the raw figure, through one shared helper rather than a patch per call site - there were ten sum sites and fixing one is how this kind of error persists. Nemotron-CC-v2 contains v1, stated by NVIDIA, so the contained row is dropped from the sum outright. The code row is 747.4B, from its own dataset card. Stage 3 now reads 55.4T raw, 11.1T-22.2T after dedup, 66-132% of a 16.8T budget - a possible shortfall where it read 363% of budget.
why:
Risk R01 has been on this page throughout, severity high, called "the single most likely schedule-breaker": 60-80% cross-corpus duplication, because every large corpus here is a differently-filtered view of the same crawls. FineWeb is 96 Common Crawl dumps, FinePDFs 106 of them, Nemotron-CC is Common Crawl, HPLT v3.0 is 45% Common Crawl by volume. The plan summed them anyway and reported the total as available supply, which is the error R01 exists to warn about. Two distinct mechanisms now do the work and they are not interchangeable: exact containment is subtracted, because a publisher stated it; unknown overlap gets a range, because nobody has measured it. Facts get subtracted, uncertainty gets a band, and per-pair overlap coefficients are not invented to make the arithmetic look more precise than the evidence.

The Indic pool needed a different answer and is treated separately. R01's range is about Common Crawl, and Sangraha's verified portion is scraped from human-checked sites, OCR and transcription - sources a crawl does not reach - which is why it is the verified portion. What is unmeasured there is narrower: Sangraha Verified and IndicCorp v2 are both AI4Bharat scrapes of Indian websites with no published cross-deduplication, so 84.9B is a ceiling rather than a count, and the page says so.
source: risk R01; NVIDIA Nemotron-CC-v2 and Nemotron-Pretraining-Code-v1 dataset cards; FineWeb, FinePDFs and HPLT 3.0 documentation; IndicLLMSuite arXiv:2403.06350

before: Chart labels were truncated with an ellipsis. Fourteen across the page were losing text, up to 82px of it: "natural Indic we h...", and every tool name in the cleaning chapter, which appears nowhere else on the page.
after: Labels wrap. Where a grid had a fixed or auto track beside a flexible one, the flexible column was absorbing the whole shortfall and reaching zero - 4px at 900px, 28px at 1180px, which stacks letters vertically and is worse than the truncation. The rows now collapse on a container query against their own column rather than the viewport.
why: An ellipsis is honest only when the full text is reachable another way. A catalogue row is a button that opens the dataset's five gates, so it keeps its ellipsis; a chart label has no such escape and the information is simply gone. The container query matters because the figure column is narrow in two disjoint viewport bands - 761-1080px, and again above 1180px where the fixed rail takes 260px - so breakpoints fixed one and left the other. Asking whether there is room in this box holds at widths nobody thought to test.
source: measured in this repository across 390-1600px

before: The catalogue said nothing about how its datasets relate to each other. FineWeb's 15T sat beside FineWeb-Edu's 1.3T with nothing to say the second is inside the first, and the same for FinePDFs and FinePDFs-Edu, and for Nemotron-CC and its v2. A reader adding any of those pairs would be double-counting and the page gave them no way to know.
after: Fifteen datasets carry a published relationship, in four kinds that are deliberately not interchangeable: contained_by (3 pairs, stated by their publishers, subtracted from any sum holding the parent), additional_to (1, recorded because Nemotron-CC-v2.1 is genuinely additive and should not be 'fixed' into a containment), shares_source (7, real overlap of unpublished size), and independent (2, because 'these do not overlap' is as much a finding as the reverse). Two are unknown. Each carries a note stating what is concretely known - crawl counts, date ranges, modality - and the citation for it, both shown on hover beside the dataset's name. The containment map the sums use is read from these records rather than hand-kept, so the label a reader sees and the arithmetic are one statement.
why: Where the relationship is published it is recorded exactly; where only the existence of overlap is published, the label says so and the magnitude comes from risk R01's range alone. No per-pair overlap coefficient is invented, because nobody has measured one and a made-up fraction wearing the authority of a computation would be worse than the honest band. The callouts carry what can be said instead: FinePDFs draws on the same 106 Common Crawl dumps as FineWeb but takes the PDFs rather than the HTML, so its overlap is far smaller than the shared source implies; CulturaX is not built from the crawl directly but from mC4 and OSCAR, which both were; Sangraha's unverified portion comes from 'existing multilingual corpora', unnamed and unresolvable, which is why it is excluded rather than modelled.
source: dataset cards for fineweb, fineweb-edu, finepdfs, finepdfs-edu, Nemotron-CC-v2, Nemotron-CC-v2.1, Nemotron-Pretraining-Code-v1, CulturaX, sangraha, IndicCorpV2; arXiv:2511.01066 (HPLT 3.0); arXiv:2403.06350 (IndicLLMSuite)

before: Two blocks in the bundle declared one provenance over a mixture of exact counts and estimated sums, and both resolved it downward. The lifecycle block was marked `estimated` because one of its seven fields, `tokens_known`, sums catalogue size estimates — so "4 of 24 post-training datasets state a size", which is counted from records we hold, rendered under the same hedge as a projection. The orphan-tier block was marked `estimated` because it prices each orphan in GPU-hours and rupees, so the claim the page actually makes from it — that every tier in the mixture has at least one test that would notice it going missing — was hedged too, though it is a match against the benchmark register and nothing more.
after: Provenance is declared at the level the figure is actually made at. The lifecycle block declares `measured` over its counts and `tokens_known` carries its own `estimated` mark inline, naming the sum it comes from. The orphan block keeps `estimated` for the costs and gains a `counts` sub-block declaring `measured` over the two figures that are matched rather than priced: how many tiers were checked, and how many have no detector.
why: Under-claiming is the safe direction of the two and that is why it survived this long, but it is not free. A provenance mark is only worth reading if it varies with the evidence; hedging a count that a miscount would make a bug rather than an estimate spends the reader's trust in the mark to buy nothing. The bare-number invariant could not catch either one — it inherits provenance down the tree and so proves only that every number carries a mark, never that the mark is the right one. Both blocks passed it before and after.
source: dataframework.sourcing.build_lifecycle; dataframework.export, orphan_tiers block

before: X26 recorded that a subset must not be summed beside the set containing it, and wired the containment map into the browser so the stage registers would apply it. The wiring never fired. `contained_by` maps a child to a *list* of parents - a dataset can sit inside more than one - and the filter tested that list for membership in a set of ids, which is false for every list there has ever been. So every stage's reachable total was the plain sum: Nemotron-CC v1's 6.30T counted once on its own and again inside Nemotron-CC-v2's 6.60T, and the same for FineWeb-Edu inside FineWeb and FinePDFs-Edu inside FinePDFs wherever a stage reached both. The comment above the line described the subtraction correctly throughout.
after: The filter asks whether any one of a child's parents is present, which is the rule the multiple-parent case needs and the rule the comment always claimed. The Python guard that proves a subset is never summed with its parent had passed all along, because the summing happens in the browser and the guard was only ever pointed at the bundle.
why: The lesson is not the array-versus-scalar slip, it is where the guard was aimed. A test that watches the producer cannot see a consumer that ignores what the producer ships. The map was correct in data.json for as long as the page was wrong on screen, and nothing in the suite could tell the two apart.
source: web/chapters.js, dropContained in the stage register; data.sourcing.contained_by

before: The catalogue described availability in prose copied from a seed cell, and 'open' in that cell turned out to mean three different things: fetch it freely, click through terms, or ask a person at the publisher and wait. Nothing distinguished them, so datasets requiring NVIDIA's approval sat in the same band as ones you can wget. Two figures were wrong as a result. COD-02 was one row covering Nemotron-Pretraining-Code v1, v2 and v3 and counted 747.4B as committable today - but v1 and v2 are gated on manual approval, and v3, the only ungated one, holds 173B and says it is incremental to the other two. And ENG-11 was 'Dolma' with no version and no size while AI2 had shipped Dolma 3, a 6T ungated ODC-By mix, so a corpus larger than anything in the committable band counted as nothing at all.
after: Each dataset's distribution point is read from the publisher rather than the seed row, and carries HuggingFace's own three-way gating value with the date it was checked. Manual gating is a blocker distinct from the licence; click-through gating is recorded but is not a blocker, because accepting terms is something you do unilaterally. Nemotron-CC-v2 moves from one letter away to two, which is the honest answer to why the older v1 is the committable one. COD-02 counts 173B. Dolma is Dolma 3 at 6T, unresolved on licence rather than invisible.
why: The page's whole dividing line is whether anybody's permission is needed, and it was sorting on a field that could not see permission. The legal chapter now also states the thing the green marks never said: a web corpus's licence covers the curation, not the copyright of the text inside it, which never left the sites it was crawled from - so a permitted mark means the curator allows redistribution of their package, not that anyone may train on its contents. Common Crawl's own terms grant use of the service, require respect for third-party copyright, demand indemnity, and advise counsel before commercial use.
source: huggingface.co/api/datasets for each row, checked 2026-08-06; nvidia/Nemotron-Pretraining-Code-v3 card ('146 M new files (173 B tokens)', 'meant to be used jointly with the v2 and v1 corpora'); allenai/dolma3_mix-6T card; commoncrawl.org/terms-of-use

before: The mix was described only by where text came from. Tiers name a provenance - english-web-hq, indic-natural - and `kind` splits them into skills and knowledge, but nothing said what a token was *for*, and nothing said what it was *about*. So the growth ladder could describe four stages without ever saying what each one teaches, and the catalogue could report 145 datasets without anyone being able to ask whether it covers news, or literature, or agriculture.
after: Two lenses added over the same tokens, deliberately not merged with the tier: a modality says what kind of thinking a token teaches, a domain says what it is about. The seven modalities and the code language list are the specification's own, carried verbatim including that agentic_traces is owned by Team 17 and its format is still pending - a modality nobody has agreed a format for cannot be collected, and the plan should say whose decision that is. Each stage of the ladder now shows the modality mix it is taught in, following the order a person is taught in: language, then the world, then symbols, then the things that need all three. General text falls 62% to 29% across the four stages while code rises 6% to 26%.
why: The coverage report is the half that matters, because it is counted rather than proposed. Of 16 domains the curriculum names, 12 have a dataset that isolates them, 2 (social, qa) exist only as an unseparated slice of a web crawl - trainable but not weightable, measurable or holdable-out - and 2 have nothing in the catalogue at all: agriculture and health. Agriculture is the uncomfortable one for an India-first model, being the sector most of the country works in. Counting only what could be committed today rather than what is catalogued, 2 of the 16 domains have even one dataset clear of every blocker. Each row ships the pattern it was matched by, so the count is checkable rather than asserted. The tier weights and curriculum emphases are typed `estimated` and named as this framework's proposal: nobody has classified a crawl by modality, and a plan dressed as a measurement would be the exact failure this register exists to catch.
source: dataframework.modalities; counted from catalog.json at build time
